title: α-Particle Scattering — Experimental Detail and Numericals
topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: A close-up of the α-scattering experiment itself: the apparatus, the counting data, and the two quantitative results (distance of closest approach and the scattering law) that NEB numericals are built on. The full model and its limitations are in the main note.
• α-source: radium C (polonium) in a lead block — lead absorbs all radiation except the fine beam escaping the collimator hole; α-particles emerge with KE ≈ 5.5 MeV and speed ≈ 1.6 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
• Foil: gold, ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁵ cm (≈ 10⁻⁷ m) thick ≈ 1000 atomic layers; gold is chosen because it is the most malleable metal and Z = 79 gives maximum deflection (∝ Z).
• Detector: circular ZnS screen; every α-hit gives a scintillation counted through a low-power microscope that can rotate about the foil through 0°–180°.
• Enclosure evacuated so α-particles are not absorbed by air (their range in air is only a few cm).
• Nearly all α-particles (≈ 99.86%) pass straight through — no deflection.
• About 1 in 8000 is deflected by more than 90°; about 1 in 10⁴–10⁶ comes straight back (θ ≈ 180°).
• The probability of scattering at angle θ falls as sin⁻⁴(θ/2) — from 0° to 180° the count falls by about 10 orders of magnitude.

At the turning point all kinetic energy is stored as electrostatic potential energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=\frac{2Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r_{0}}$, giving $r_{0}=\frac{2Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}(KE)}$. For 5.5 MeV α on gold r₀ ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m — about 40 nuclear radii, so the α-particle never touches the nucleus and the nucleus acts as a point charge. This number is an **upper limit** of the nuclear size, which is why the experiment 'measures' the nucleus without seeing it.
### Impact parameter (the other half of the story)

The scattering angle is fixed by the impact parameter b (the perpendicular distance the α-particle's initial line would pass from the nucleus): $b=\frac{kZe^{2}}{KE}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}$. Head-on approach (b = 0) gives θ = 180° (back-scattering); large b gives tiny θ — the geometric origin of the sin⁻⁴ law.
• Undeflected majority → atom mostly empty space.
• Large-angle deflection → a concentrated positive charge much heavier than the α-particle (a light electron cannot turn a 7300-times-heavier projectile).
• Back-scattering → the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a volume 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom.
confusion: ❌ The foil must be thick for good scattering. ✅ It must be extremely thin (≈1000 atoms) so an α-particle meets at most a few nuclei; a thick foil would absorb the particles.
❌ Electrons deflect the α-particles. ✅ Electron mass is ≈1/7300 of the α-mass, so momentum transfer is negligible; only the nucleus can scatter.
❌ r₀ is the nuclear radius. ✅ It is the distance of closest approach — an upper limit; the nuclear radius is ≈10⁻¹⁵ m, ten times smaller.

universalFacts: ≈1 in 8000 α-particles was deflected by more than 90°; the count falls by ~10 orders of magnitude from 0° to 180°.
For 5.5 MeV α on gold, r₀ ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m ≈ 40 nuclear radii.
Scattering probability scales as Z² of the foil and as 1/(KE)² of the α-particle.
examples: **Problem:** α-particles of 4 MeV approach silver (Z = 47). Find r₀. **Solution:** r₀ = 2kZe²/KE = (2 × 9×10⁹ × 47 × (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)²)/(4 × 1.6×10⁻¹³) ≈ 3.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m — the measurement is a nucleus-size upper limit, not the radius itself.
importantNotes: State clearly that r₀ is an upper limit to nuclear size — a favourite distinction question.

summary: This tab drills the Geiger–Marsden α-scattering experiment itself — the radium-C source in a lead block with its collimator, the gold foil only ≈4 × 10⁻⁵ cm (≈1000 atomic layers) thick, the rotatable ZnS scintillation screen and the evacuated enclosure — together with the counting data (≈99.86% undeflected, about 1 in 8000 beyond 90°, roughly 1 in 10⁴–10⁶ back-scattered, counts falling as 1/sin⁴(θ/2)) and the two quantitative results NEB numericals are built on. The distance of closest approach, r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m for a 5.5 MeV α-particle on gold, and the impact parameter b = (kZe²/KE)·cot(θ/2), turn those observations into numbers. Each observation is tied to its inference — mostly empty space, a heavy concentrated positive charge, a nucleus occupying only ≈10⁻¹⁵ of the atomic volume — while r₀ is read correctly as an upper limit on nuclear size, never as the radius itself.
importantConcepts: α-scattering apparatus: radium-C source, lead block with collimator, gold foil, rotatable ZnS screen with microscope, vacuum enclosure
Geiger–Marsden counting data: ≈99.86% undeflected, 1 in 8000 beyond 90°, very few back-scattered at 180°
Rutherford scattering law N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2), with counts falling ≈10 orders of magnitude from 0° to 180°
Distance of closest approach r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) as an experimental upper limit on nuclear size
Impact parameter b = (kZe²/KE)·cot(θ/2) linking scattering angle to trajectory geometry
Scattering probability proportional to Z² of the foil and to 1/(KE)² of the projectile
importantStatements: The gold foil must be extremely thin (≈4 × 10⁻⁵ cm) so an α-particle meets at most a few nuclei; a thick foil would absorb the particles.
Only the nucleus can deflect α-particles: the electron has ≈1/7300 of the α-particle's mass, so momentum transfer from it is negligible.
r₀ is the distance of closest approach, an upper limit on the nuclear radius (≈10⁻¹⁵ m) — not the radius itself.
The number of scattered particles falls by about 10 orders of magnitude as the angle goes from 0° to 180°.
Lead absorbs all radiation from the source except the fine beam escaping through the collimator hole.
The experiment is carried out in vacuum because the range of α-particles in air is only a few centimetres.

keyPoints: ≈99.86% pass straight through → the atom is mostly empty space.
≈1 in 8000 is deflected by more than 90° → charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny, heavy centre.
About 1 in 10⁴–10⁶ returns near 180° → nuclear volume is only ≈10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume.
N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2): the scattering probability collapses as the angle grows.
r₀ ∝ Z/KE: heavier nuclei and slower α-particles give larger closest approaches.
For a 5.5 MeV α-particle on gold, r₀ ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m ≈ 40 nuclear radii.
specialNotes: Since r₀ exceeds the nuclear radius for these α-particles, the nucleus acts as a point charge and no capture occurs.
Gold is chosen for two reasons at once — it can be beaten extremely thin and Z = 79 maximises the deflection, which is proportional to Z.
A thicker foil is not 'better': it simply stops the α-particles, so thinness is the compromise between transmission and the number of nuclei met.
Because the scattering is done by the nucleus, the result is independent of the chemical state of the foil.
Head-on collisions (b = 0) are the rarest, since only α-particles aimed within a nuclear diameter are turned back.
examShortTricks: Read 1/sin⁴(θ/2) as 'sin⁴ of HALF the angle' — sin(θ/2) → 1 as θ → 180°, which is why back-scattering is rarest.
r₀ = 2kZe²/KE; if KE is given in eV multiply by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹, and dropping the 2 halves the answer.
Whenever nuclear size is asked, write 'distance of closest approach — an upper limit' as a single phrase.
Quote the 1/7300 mass ratio to kill the 'electrons deflect the α-particles' option instantly.
Head-on → 180°, large b → tiny θ: that one line gives the whole impact-parameter story.
examNotes: A labelled diagram plus the observation → conclusion mapping is a standard 4–5 mark question; the marks lie in the inference chain, not in listing the apparatus.
The two numericals built on this experiment are r₀ and b; both require KE in joules and the correct Z inserted.
One-mark questions frequently ask the fraction scattered beyond 90° (1 in 8000) or the way scattering depends on Z.
Expect a 'why thin foil / why vacuum / why lead block' trio as a 3-mark part question.
